title: Applied scenario: Mateo's revision
stem: Mateo is preparing for his exams. He reads his notes again and again the night before each test, while messaging friends and listening to podcasts. He says the material "feels familiar" but he often goes blank in the exam room. His teacher suggests a different approach.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why Mateo's current approach may not be effective, using one cognitive theory or model.
markscheme: theory identified, e.g. cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988) / working memory model
applied: messaging and podcasts add extraneous load / compete for the phonological loop while reading
less capacity remains for processing and transferring material to long-term memory
supporting evidence, e.g. Ophir et al. (2009) multitaskers filter distraction poorly / Landry & Bartling (2011) articulatory suppression
familiarity from rereading is not the same as being able to retrieve, explaining going blank

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Suggest how Mateo could improve his recall, with reference to research.
markscheme: use retrieval practice / self-testing instead of rereading
evidence: Roediger & Karpicke (2006) testing produced better recall after a week than restudying
space sessions over several days rather than cramming
evidence: spacing effect, e.g. Cepeda et al. (2006) meta-analysis
remove distractions to reduce cognitive load
each suggestion is explicitly linked to Mateo's situation
